Pertain means to be connected to, related to, or concerned with something. When something pertains to a topic or subject, it belongs to that world — it has a relevant link or connection to it.

Think of it this way: imagine a large circle drawn around a subject. Anything that falls inside that circle pertains to it. Anything outside the circle does not.

"Pertain" carries the same core idea across all its uses, but it shows up in three slightly different shades depending on context.

Shade 1 — To relate to or be about something

This is by far the most common use. When something pertains to a topic, it is about that topic, or is directly relevant to it.

  • The new rules pertain to all employees, not just managers.

(= The new rules are about / apply to / concern all employees.)

  • Please share only information that pertains to the investigation.

(= Share only information that is directly related to the investigation.)

  • This chapter pertains to climate change and its effects on agriculture.

(= This chapter is about / concerns climate change and agriculture.)

You can often replace "pertain to" with "relate to," "concern," or "be about" — and the meaning stays the same.

Shade 2 — To belong to something as a part of it

Here, "pertain" means that something is naturally part of or attached to something else — like a feature, a quality, or a right that goes along with it.

  • The responsibilities pertaining to this job are many.

(= The responsibilities that come with this job / that belong to this job.)

  • She claimed the rights pertaining to her citizenship.

(= The rights that belong to / go along with her citizenship.)

Think of it as: the thing doesn't just relate to something — it actually belongs to it, like an accessory or a built-in feature.

Shade 3 — To be appropriate or fitting for a situation

This shade is less common, but it exists. It means something is suitable or proper for a given situation or role.

  • He was asked to conduct himself in a manner pertaining to his position.

(= In a manner appropriate to / fitting for his position.)

This shade is quite formal and mostly found in older or official writing.

"Pertain" is almost always followed by "to."

You do not say: "This issue pertains the contract."
You say: "This issue pertains to the contract."

The word "to" is its permanent companion in nearly every sentence.
How It Feels in Real Life (Register)

"Pertain" is a formal word. You will see it frequently in:

  • Legal documents ("all matters pertaining to the agreement...")
  • Academic writing ("evidence pertaining to the hypothesis...")
  • Official reports and professional communication

In everyday conversation, people are far more likely to say "related to," "about," or "concerning" instead. If you are talking casually with a friend, saying "pertain" might sound stiff or overly formal. But in writing — especially professional or academic writing — it is a perfectly natural and respected word.

These words are close in meaning to "pertain to," but not always interchangeable:

  • Relate to — the most common, everyday alternative. Almost always safe to swap in.
  • Concern — similar, but slightly more active. "This concerns you" has a slightly more urgent or direct feel.
  • Apply to — used specifically when a rule, law, or policy is relevant to something or someone.
  • Refer to — this is about pointing at something or making reference to it, not always about being connected to it. Slightly different angle.
  • Be relevant to — highlights that something matters or is useful in the context of something else.

When in doubt, "pertain to" = "relate to." That swap works in almost every situation.

A Few Final Examples to Cement It

• Submit only documents pertaining to your application. (= relevant to your application)
  • The laws pertaining to data privacy have changed. (= the laws concerning / about data privacy)
  • He refused to answer questions not pertaining to the case. (= not connected to the case)
  • The duties pertaining to the role are outlined below. (= the duties belonging to / that come with the role)

Once you recognize that "pertain to" = "be connected/related/relevant/belonging to," you will understand it correctly in any sentence you encounter.
